question: Why do people today seem busier than in the past?
answer: One reason is technology. Because we can be contacted at any time by email or messaging apps, work often follows us home, so the line between work and free time has become blurred. question: Is being busy a sign of success?
answer: In many cultures, people do treat busyness as a status symbol – saying 'I'm so busy' can be a way of showing that you're important. But I don't think it's a reliable sign of success. Some very successful people are good at delegating and protecting their free time, while some people are busy simply because they're disorganised or can't say no. I'd argue that real success is achieving your goals while still having time for your health, family and interests. Being constantly busy can actually be a sign that something is wrong.

question: What can employers do to help their staff manage stress?

question: What is the best way to stay motivated when working towards a long-term goal?
answer: I think breaking the goal into smaller milestones is the most effective strategy, because each small success gives you a sense of progress. Having support from other people also helps – for example, joining a group or telling friends about your goal makes you more accountable. It's also important to accept that setbacks are normal. question: What are the main reasons people are late?
answer: I think there are several reasons. Sometimes it's not their fault – for example, traffic jams, delayed trains or bad weather. But often, people don't plan well. answer: I'd say the most important quality is the ability to explain things clearly in different ways, because every student learns differently. question: Do you think the role of teachers will change in the future because of technology?
answer: I'm fairly sure it will. As artificial intelligence becomes capable of delivering information and even marking work, teachers will probably spend less time lecturing and more time acting as guides or mentors – helping students evaluate information, work collaboratively and develop critical thinking. question: Why do so few young people want to become teachers in some countries?
answer: There are several interconnected reasons. In many countries, teachers' salaries haven't kept pace with other professions that require a similar level of education, so it's financially less attractive. The workload is also notoriously heavy – lesson planning, marking and administration often extend well into evenings and weekends.
